1.pericope_label: The people complain at Taberah and the fire of the LORD burns among them

schools.summary: Gill canvasses the guesses at the cause and cites Jarchi for a people seeking a pretext to break with God; Calvin turns the question into one of grammar, rejects four renderings of the participle in favour of fainting, and reads the cry to Moses rather than to God as the mark of a conscience that dares not look at him.

Henry supposes the complainers had no common grievance and that discontent always finds one, matches the fire of their wrath against the fire of God's, and takes their sudden recourse to Moses as the way men claim in distress the friends they slighted in prosperity.

Clarke reports Jerome's conjecture about the length of the way, offers three natural or supernatural accounts of the fire, and insists it must have reached every murmurer; Wesley grounds the complaint in three days of howling wilderness and reads the sparing of the camp's centre as mercy.

Keil and Delitzsch refuse to name a cause and describe the fire as sent by God without issuing directly from him as in Leviticus; Ellicott sharpens the rendering of the opening clause, suggests the simoom, and notes the greater severity of judgments after the law was given.

debates: What the people were complaining of, and whether the fire reached only the outskirts of the camp
outliers: Calvin rejects the common rendering of the participle as murmuring in favour of fainting, and dismisses 'seeking occasion' as far fetched

4.pericope_label: The mixed multitude lust for flesh, and the manna is described

schools.summary: Gill identifies the mixed multitude with the Targum's proselytes and supports the Egyptian fare from Herodotus and Diodorus while insisting Israel paid dearly for it; Calvin traces the contagion from the strangers to the whole people, hears the list of vegetables as humble fare fondly praised rather than luxury, and answers that God was angry not at the desire for flesh but at the disobedience, intemperance and ingratitude wrapped around it.

Henry makes the hangers-on the leaven that leavened the lump, contrasts the remembered cucumbers with the forgotten brick-kilns, describes the manna as bread costing neither money nor care, and lays down that no desire should be indulged which cannot in faith be turned into prayer.

Clarke glosses the term for the mixed multitude, calls them demi-infidels, and defends the Egyptian delicacies as genuinely fine in that country; Wesley explains the cheapness of fish by the Egyptians' own religious scruples and notes that Israel's cattle were too few and reserved for breeding.

Keil and Delitzsch trace the impulse to the mob and hear in they wept again a backward reference to the earlier complaint in the wilderness of Sin; Ellicott derives the word for the mixed multitude, details the Egyptian produce, restricts freely to the fish and reads it as gratuitous, and treats the craving as typical of man's repugnance to the gospel.

debates: Whether the longing for flesh was itself sinful, and what 'freely' means of the fish of Egypt

10.pericope_label: Moses hears the people weep and remonstrates with God

schools.summary: Calvin treats the weeping as self-inflicted misery, judges Moses' zeal holy but his excess an error, calls the question about conceiving the people inconsiderate against a divine calling, and names the request for death the grossest fault of all; Gill defends Moses' fatherhood in a civil sense and notes that he was never in fact alone.
Henry grants the provocation and still finds Moses undervaluing his honour, magnifying his own performance, and distrusting a grace that could have carried a far heavier work.

Wesley reads the complaint as a reproach that God had not excused him earlier, presses the point that Israel were not his children, and traces the dread of wretchedness to the fear that their destruction would make Moses and God alike look like impostors.

Keil and Delitzsch distinguish the discontent of despair, which still prays, from the murmuring of unbelief, which does not, and parse the request for death as an uninterrupted killing; Ellicott links the verb for displeased to the verb for afflicted, marks the emphatic pronouns, and reports the scribal alteration of my wretchedness for Thy.

debates: Whether Moses' remonstrance was a fault, and how far it treats the people's demand as reasonable
outliers: Ellicott reports that 'my wretchedness' is one of the eighteen passages the scribes are said to have altered, substituting my for Thy

16.pericope_label: The seventy elders promised, the month of flesh threatened, and Moses doubts

schools.summary: Gill notes that God answers without upbraiding, reads Moses' objection as distrust of God's power, and cites the Targum's rendering of it; Calvin takes the call to sanctify themselves as irony chastising gluttony, builds his case on the clause about despising a God present among them, and names two faults in Moses' doubt, a failure simply to trust and an attempt to measure God's power by his own senses.

Henry sees God's goodness drawing occasion from man's badness, explains why Moses rather than the people chose the seventy, treats the promised month as a threat that exposes the vanity of sensual delight, and observes that Moses looked for bulky creatures where small birds would serve.

Clarke reports the patristic figure of the lamp lit from a lamp, resists the rabbinic derivation of the Sanhedrin from this passage, and asks pointedly whether Moses lost gifts he had undervalued; Wesley holds the spirit came to the seventy directly from God, reads the sanctifying as a call to repentance, and explains why this act of distrust went unpunished where a later one did not.

Keil and Delitzsch defend the justice of Moses' complaint as zeal for an office too heavy for one man; Ellicott cites Rashi on the undiminished lamp, notes that the request was granted in judgment more than mercy, compares the single day of the earlier quails, and reads the question about flocks and fish as natural hyperbole.

debates: Whether Moses lost anything of his own gifts when the spirit was given to the seventy
outliers: Calvin reads the command to sanctify themselves as ironic rebuke rather than a genuine call to purification

24.pericope_label: The seventy prophesy, and Eldad and Medad in the camp

schools.summary: Calvin measures Moses' recovery by his prompt obedience, holds the gift of prophecy temporary and merely credentialing, thinks Eldad and Medad were simply never found by the summons and that God arranged their absence so the common people could witness the miracle, and finds in Moses' reply the gentleness of a man indifferent to his own dignity; Gill passes on the rabbinic identification of the young man as Gershom.

Henry has Moses composed again by communion with God, reads Eldad and Medad's absence as modesty that was still disobedience and yet proved the Spirit to be God's gift, and draws from the rebuke of Joshua four rules against envying gifts, against heat over infirmities, against party spirit, and against silencing those who do not follow with us.

Clarke grounds prophesying in a verb meaning to pray and entreat and answers the episode with Charles Wesley's hymns upon it; Wesley notes the seventy are still so called though two were missing, holds the Spirit's abode with them perpetual because the use of the gift was, and marks that Moses wished all were prophets and not all rulers.

Keil and Delitzsch read the elders as ranged in a semicircle before the tent, infer from those who were written that the summons was issued in writing and that Israel had learned the art in Egypt, and explain Joshua's protest from his standing as Moses' servant; Ellicott denies that the phrase requires a full circle, argues the word prophesy need not mean prediction, and reads the whole as teaching the freeness of the Spirit.

debates: Whether the seventy kept the gift of prophecy or received it once as a credential
outliers: Wesley and Calvin read the same clause in opposite senses, Wesley that they did not cease and Calvin that they prophesied no more

31.pericope_label: The quails, the plague, and the graves of lust

schools.summary: Calvin fixes on the timing of the stroke, that God struck while the meat was in their mouths rather than waiting for satiety to turn to disgust, since a swollen belly never appeases the lust of eating; Gill harmonises the winds of the psalm into one south-east wind.

Henry reads the gathering as a portrait of appetite and sets it against David refusing water won at hazard, and explains the sequence of satiety before plague both as protecting God's reputation for power and as the meaning of the prosperity of sinners, who are fed as an ox before the slaughter.

Clarke denies the quails lay heaped on the ground, supports the natural history from Hasselquist and Maillet, refuses to specify a plague the writer left unspecified, and turns the whole to the danger of prayers that would ruin us if granted; Wesley defends the ten homers on four grounds and explains why the same murmuring was spared in Exodus and punished here.

Keil and Delitzsch trace the wind and the migration, reject the theory that the quails' own flesh was toxic in favour of an extraordinary judgment, and dispute the usual identification of Hazeroth on the Hebrew root; Ellicott lays out both readings of the two cubits, gives the size of a homer, and holds the natural and the supernatural to be combined in the plague.

debates: Whether the quails lay two cubits deep on the ground or flew two cubits above it, and whether the plague had a natural cause
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch reject the toxic-quail explanation that Ellicott's account of a natural surfeit comes close to accepting
